title: Chevron Stock Price Forecast: CVX Slips to $188 as Oil's 20% Drop From Its Highs Bites - TradingNEWS
content: Chevron is a leveraged bet on the Strait of Hormuz wearing a dividend aristocrat's suit, and right now those two identities are pulling against each other. The stock rode crude from $60 to $100 as the Iran war choked off Gulf supply, and it's now sliding as oil gives back 20% of that move on ceasefire hopes — and because Chevron carries more oil leverage than its integrated peers, it feels every dollar of that decline more than almost anyone. CVX traded near $188 on June 5, down about 0.45% premarket and well off its $214.71 high, drifting with the falling crude price. But underneath sits a fortress: a 39-year dividend growth streak, more than $15 billion in annual free cash flow, and a forward earnings multiple near 14x. The stock is hostage to oil, but the dividend is the floor that pure crude doesn't have. The two forces defining Chevron are simple and opposed. On one side, CVX is among the most oil-levered of the integrated majors, which means its earnings and share price swing harder with crude than more diversified peers — it's the high-beta way to play the energy complex. On the other side, it's one of the market's most reliable income stocks, with a dividend streak stretching back nearly four decades and a balance sheet built to defend that payout through cycles. You're buying commodity volatility and income stability in the same ticker. Right now the volatility side is winning the tape. Crude has dropped roughly 20% from its 2026 highs on optimism that a U.S.-Iran ceasefire reopens the Strait of Hormuz, and Chevron's greater oil leverage leaves it more at risk in a falling-crude environment than its peers. That's why CVX has drifted from its $214 high toward $188 even as the broader market churns. The dividend and the cheap forward multiple are the counterweight — the reason the stock has a floor that a barrel of oil doesn't. The whole forecast comes down to which force dominates from here, and that depends almost entirely on what crude does next. Put numbers on it. Chevron traded near $188 to $189 on June 5, off about 0.45% in premarket action, having opened recent sessions lower as oil softened. The stock sits well below its 52-week high of $214.71 but comfortably above the $133.77 low, a range that captures the full round-trip of the oil war — Chevron bottomed near those lows in late 2025 when WTI sat around $60, then recovered hard as crude rocketed to $100 on the Hormuz disruption. The market cap sits around $371 billion, keeping CVX firmly among the largest energy companies on the planet and the second-largest U.S. oil major. The pullback from $214 to $188 is the oil-price decline showing up in the equity. As WTI slid from its $100-plus peak back toward $92 on ceasefire optimism, Chevron gave back a chunk of its war-driven rally. The stock is now in the lower-middle of its 52-week range, leaning with the crude tape but holding well above its lows. That positioning matters: CVX isn't cheap relative to its trough, but it's discounted relative to its peak, and the gap between the two is almost entirely the oil-price story playing out in real time. The immediate pressure on Chevron is the crude price, and the math is direct. WTI surged from roughly $60 at the start of the year to a peak above $100 as the Strait of Hormuz closure tightened global supply, and Chevron's shares surged with it. Now crude has reversed about 20% from those highs — WTI near $92, Brent near $95 — as a 60-day U.S.-Iran ceasefire memorandum took shape and traders priced the strait reopening. Every dollar of that crude decline flows through to Chevron's upstream earnings, which is the bulk of where it makes money. The leverage cuts sharper for Chevron than for its peers. Its earnings mix skews more toward upstream oil production than some more balanced integrated rivals, so it has greater oil leverage and therefore more downside in a falling-crude environment. That's the trade-off for the upside it captured on the way up. The stock that rode the war premium higher now wears the ceasefire discount, and as long as the peace narrative dominates the oil tape, Chevron faces a headwind that its dividend and buybacks can cushion but not erase. The crude price is the single biggest variable in the CVX forecast. Here's where the oil setup makes Chevron interesting rather than just bearish. The crude market is pricing peace while the physical market is screaming tight — the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed, U.S. inventories have drawn for six straight weeks toward minimum operating levels, and the global market is strongly undersupplied. That disconnect means oil is hostage to a binary: either the ceasefire gets signed and crude falls toward $80 and the $60s, or the talks stall, the strait stays shut, and crude snaps back toward $106 and beyond. Chevron is a leveraged expression of exactly that binary. If peace breaks out, CVX faces continued downside as crude falls and its oil-heavy earnings compress. If the ceasefire collapses — more missiles into the Gulf, a Hezbollah rejection, no Trump sign-off — crude rips higher and Chevron's upstream cash flow explodes, sending the stock back toward and through its $214 high. That's the asymmetry: the stock has already priced a good chunk of the peace scenario by sliding to $188, which means a ceasefire failure is arguably more of an upside catalyst for CVX than a ceasefire success is a downside one. Chevron is the equity way to bet on the strait staying shut. While the share price rides the crude rollercoaster, the dividend is the anchor, and it's a formidable one. Chevron has grown its dividend for 39 consecutive years, a streak that puts it among the most reliable income payers in the entire market and signals a management commitment to the payout that survives oil-price cycles. The current yield sits around 3.7%, with the most recent quarterly dividend carrying an ex-date of May 19 and a payment date of June 10. That income stream is backed by more than $15 billion in annual free cash flow and a long record of returning over $5 billion per quarter to shareholders through combined dividends and buybacks. There's one caveat worth flagging: on a trailing basis, the dividend isn't fully covered by earnings, with a payout ratio around 103%. That sounds alarming in isolation, but it's largely an artifact of depressed trailing earnings — Chevron's Q1 results were hit by mark-to-market derivative timing effects given the quarter's extreme oil volatility, which dented reported profit without reflecting the underlying cash generation. The free cash flow that actually funds the dividend remains robust at $15 billion-plus. Still, a payout ratio over 100% means the dividend's long-term safety depends on oil staying high enough to keep cash flow strong, which ties the income story right back to the Hormuz binary. The dividend is a fortress, but its moat is the crude price. Chevron's valuation tells two completely different stories depending on which earnings number you use, and the gap is the key to the bull case. On a trailing basis, the stock trades at a price-to-earnings multiple north of 32x — which screams expensive for an oil major and would normally be a red flag. But that trailing figure is distorted by the Q1 derivative timing noise that crushed reported earnings without touching the cash engine. It's an accounting artifact, not a reflection of how the business is actually performing. On a forward basis, the picture flips entirely. Analysts forecast Chevron's 2026 earnings per share near $13.86, with estimates ranging from $8.33 to $18.97, which puts the forward P/E around 14x at a $188 share price. That's a normal-to-cheap multiple for a high-quality integrated major with a fortress dividend and a 27%-plus forecast earnings growth rate. The valuation split is the crux of the bull thesis: the stock looks expensive on backward-looking, distorted earnings and cheap on forward, normalized ones. Investors who look through the Q1 noise see a discounted energy giant; those who anchor on the trailing multiple see an overpriced one. The forward number is the one that matters, and it argues CVX has value here. Chevron's biggest strategic move is now embedded in the story: the completed merger with Hess. The integration is far enough along that leadership transitions are flowing through, with a senior Hess Integration executive bringing more than 35 years of oil and gas experience set to take on an expanded role. The deal reshapes Chevron's portfolio, adding higher-margin production volumes and prized assets that improve the company's long-term growth and returns profile. The strategic logic is about quality, not just scale. Management's path to improving returns and free cash flow runs through disciplined capital spending, cost reductions, and the addition of those higher-margin Hess barrels — a combination meant to lift the company's cash generation per barrel rather than simply pumping more. Chevron already produces 3.7 million barrels of oil equivalent per day with 1.8 million barrels of daily refining capacity and 10.6 billion barrels of proved reserves, and the Hess assets bolster that base with growth that compounds over years. The merger is the structural upgrade underneath the cyclical oil-price noise, and it's a meaningful piece of why analysts have been lifting their targets. Chevron isn't standing still on new exploration, either. The company filed a request to take a stake of more than 70% in an offshore block southwest of Greece from a Greek energy partner, expanding its Mediterranean footprint. It's also moving into Syria, partnering with Qatar's UCC Holding on an inaugural offshore deep-water oil and gas exploration project as the region opens to development. These are early-stage, long-dated bets, but they signal a company actively rebuilding its exploration pipeline rather than simply harvesting existing assets. These expansion moves matter for the multi-year story even if they don't move the needle this quarter. New frontier acreage in the Mediterranean and Middle East gives Chevron optionality on future production growth, which is exactly what a major needs to sustain its reserve base and justify its long-term value. Combined with the Hess barrels, the project pipeline gives analysts something to underwrite beyond the current oil price — a reason to look past the crude cycle toward sustained cash generation. The growth-beyond-core narrative is part of why the Street's targets cluster well above the current share price. Not every signal is bullish, and the ownership data carries a warning. Berkshire Hathaway reduced its Chevron stake by about 35%, raising roughly $8 billion while still remaining a significant holder with a 4.2% position. When the most famous value investor in the world trims a third of a position, the market notices — though it's worth weighing against the fact that Berkshire still holds billions in CVX and the trim may reflect portfolio reshaping as much as a view on Chevron specifically. It's a yellow flag, not a red one. The insider activity reinforces the caution. Company insiders have sold roughly $200 million more than they bought over the past 12 months through options and on-market transactions, with continued selling in recent months. Insider selling is always noisy — executives sell for countless personal reasons unrelated to their view of the stock — but a net $200 million skew toward selling, combined with Berkshire's trim, suggests those closest to the company aren't aggressively adding at current levels. It doesn't override the forward valuation or the dividend, but it's a data point the bulls have to acknowledge: the insiders and the largest holder are reducing, not accumulating. In the integrated-major hierarchy, Chevron is the clear number two in the U.S. behind ExxonMobil, and the comparison frames the investment case. Exxon is larger and somewhat more diversified across chemicals and downstream, which makes it marginally less oil-levered than Chevron. That means in a falling-crude environment like the current one, Chevron tends to underperform Exxon, while in a rising-crude environment, Chevron's higher leverage lets it outperform. The two trade as the twin pillars of U.S. energy, but Chevron is the more aggressive bet on the oil price itself. Against the broader peer set — ConocoPhillips and the international majors — Chevron's draw is the combination of that oil leverage with its dividend pedigree and the Hess-enhanced growth profile. The energy sector as a whole has been one of the market's swing groups in 2026, ripping on the war premium and pulling back on ceasefire hopes, and Chevron has amplified both moves. For investors choosing among the majors, the question is whether they want Chevron's higher beta to crude or a more defensive peer. With oil at a binary crossroads, that choice is essentially a directional call on the Strait of Hormuz. Technically, Chevron sits near $188, in the lower-middle of its $133.77 to $214.71 52-week range, having pulled back from the highs with crude. The stock has support from its late-2025 base and the structural floor its dividend yield provides — as the price falls, the yield rises, which tends to attract income buyers and cushion declines. Resistance sits up toward the $214 high, with the path there gated almost entirely by the oil price. Wall Street remains constructive despite the pullback. The consensus rating is a Buy, with average 12-month price targets clustering around $216, implying mid-teens upside from current levels, against a high estimate of $236 and a low of $170. Individual desks have been lifting targets on expectations for firmer long-term oil prices and the Hess-driven cash flow improvement — one major bank moved to $214 with an Overweight, another to $230. The analyst community is looking through the near-term crude wobble toward Chevron's normalized earnings power and shareholder returns, which is why the targets sit well above the $188 share price even as oil softens. The base case is range-bound trade that tracks the oil price, with CVX holding near $188 and the dividend yield providing a floor while the $214 high caps the upside. As long as crude chops between the ceasefire-driven lows and the undersupply-driven highs, Chevron drifts with it, supported underneath by its 3.7% yield, $15 billion-plus free cash flow, and a forward multiple near 14x that limits how cheap it can get. This is a stock that pays you to wait for the oil binary to resolve. The bear case is a signed 60-day ceasefire and a reopened Strait of Hormuz that drives crude toward $80 and the $60s, compressing Chevron's oil-heavy earnings and pressuring the stock back toward the lower half of its range, with the dividend's 103% trailing payout ratio coming under scrutiny if cash flow thins. The bull case is the opposite oil outcome — a collapsed ceasefire that keeps the strait shut and the market undersupplied, sending crude back toward $106-plus and Chevron's upstream cash flow surging, which would drive CVX toward the $216 consensus target and potentially the $230–$236 high estimates. The catalysts to watch are the weekend Iran negotiation headlines, weekly oil inventory data, the crude price itself, and the June 10 dividend payment. For now, Chevron is the leveraged equity bet on the Strait of Hormuz, cushioned by a fortress dividend and a cheap forward multiple — sliding with crude near $188, but carrying more upside than downside if the strait stays shut.

title: Here's How Cleaner Transportation Fuels Are Powering Valero's Growth - The Globe and Mail
content: As governments and consumers place greater emphasis on reducing emissions and improving air quality, demand for cleaner transportation fuels is expected to grow. To address the growing demand for cleaner fuels and meet low-carbon fuel standards, Valero Energy Corporation VLO is expanding its low-carbon fuels business through renewable diesel, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and ethanol, creating a diversified platform beyond traditional refining. Valero's low-carbon fuels portfolio is anchored by its Diamond Green Diesel (DGD) joint venture, which has increased renewable fuel production capacity from 160 million gallons per year in 2013 to approximately 1.2 billion gallons per year in first-quarter 2026. Since its inception, DGD has generated more than $3 billion in cumulative EBITDA. Renewable diesel is particularly attractive because it can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 80% while remaining compatible with existing fuel infrastructure. Valero strengthened its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) capacity through the Port Arthur project, which can convert up to 235 million gallons of renewable diesel into SAF annually. The project enables airlines to meet strict emission requirements while providing an attractive return that surpasses the company's 25% after-tax internal rate of return threshold. The refiner operates 12 ethanol plants producing 1.7 billion gallons of ethanol annually, benefiting from low-cost operations, export opportunities and lower-carbon incentives. Together, renewable diesel, SAF and ethanol support long-term cash flow growth and enhance VLO’s ability to capitalize on the growing demand for cleaner transportation fuels. BP plc BP and Chevron Corporation CVX are actively implementing strategies aimed at minimizing emissions and improving overall air quality. BP has developed a diversified renewable energy portfolio across solar, wind and bioenergy through strategic partnerships that enhance growth while limiting capital requirements. BP has also strengthened its presence in renewable natural gas through Archaea Energy, positioning it to benefit from rising demand for lower-carbon fuels. Chevron is actively cutting emissions by scaling up the production of renewable fuels such as biodiesel, hydrogen and renewable natural gas. To further minimize its carbon footprint, CVX is simultaneously advancing carbon capture, utilization and storage technologies to safely trap carbon dioxide underground. The CEO noted that, as the oil price is near $100 a barrel, he expects the debt to be fully repaid in a year. Wirth noted that negotiations are already underway, with Chevron, ExxonMobil, and ConocoPhillips all meeting with Venezuela’s acting government, led by Delcy Rodriguez. Moreover, US President Trump has urged US oil companies to invest $100 billion to rebuild Venezuela’s oil industry, which holds some of the world’s largest reserves. title: Bessent Calls It 'Transitory'—But Big Oil Warns Of A Catastrophic Summer Fuel Squeeze - Benzinga
content: Benzinga Rankings give you vital metrics on any stock – anytime. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent disagrees with the oil industry. In his eyes, recent energy-driven inflation and elevated crude prices are temporary distortions that will soon reverse. Some may even dare to say, transitory. Yet Chevron Corp. (NYSE:CVX) CEO Mike Wirth has been vocal about how shrinking inventories and damaged energy infrastructure are creating conditions for a longer-lasting supply crunch. Bessent has rejected pessimism, pointing to a series of strong macroeconomic indicators. Speaking during a White House briefing reported by the New York Post, he highlighted all-time highs in stock indices, resilient consumer spending, and real GDP growth of 2.6% over the past four quarters. He also argued that the recent decline in the personal savings rate should not automatically be interpreted as financial stress. "Academic literature would tell you a lower savings rate can mean one of two things: the kind of doomer view that you took, or that people have more confidence," Bessent said. He noted that average 401(k) balances have risen by roughly $30,000 since President Donald Trump returned to office, suggesting households feel more comfortable spending rather than accumulating cash savings. The Treasury secretary's broader inflation argument rests on the belief that current price pressures are overwhelmingly tied to energy markets. Despite April's 3.8% year-over-year CPI reading and a sharp rise in gasoline costs earlier this year, Bessent maintains that the inflation spike is not becoming entrenched. "I firmly believe that nothing is more transient than a supply shock," Bessent told CNBC. His confidence rests on the belief that oil flows through the region will normalize once the conflict ends. "We are more resilient to energy price fluctuations due to President Trump's energy dominance and deregulatory agenda." He has gone even further, publicly predicting that "oil will be lower than pre-conflict levels when this ends." Wirth, however, sees a far more fragile physical market beneath the reassuring macroeconomic data. Speaking at a Bernstein conference, the Chevron CEO warned that crude inventories are steadily shrinking and that the market's traditional shock absorbers are disappearing. "The buffers and the shock absorbers are being steadily drawn down, and the ability for the market to absorb this imbalance is drastically diminished today versus where we started," Wirth said, according to the Financial Times. "Over the next few weeks, we're likely to see those pressures flow through more directly to physical prices, and there's more upwards pressure that I would expect as we get into June and certainly into July." If elevated physical pressures push crude prices too high over June and July, the energy crisis risks tipping the global economy into recession, he added. The ongoing disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has removed an estimated 12 million to 13 million barrels of oil per day from global markets. According to Wirth, the market initially absorbed the shock because inventories were unusually high before the conflict and because governments released strategic reserves. Those temporary relief mechanisms are now fading. Meanwhile, ADNOC chief executive Sultan al-Jaber warned that restoring Middle Eastern energy infrastructure is unlikely to happen quickly, even if the conflict gets resolved. "It will take at least four months to get back to 80 percent of pre-conflict flows, and full flows will not return before the first or even second quarter of 2027," he said during an Atlantic Council event on May 21. © 2026 Benzinga.com. title: ExxonMobil's Permian Advantage: Low Breakeven, Rising Production - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil CorporationXOM has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. Let’s delve a little deeper into why operating in the Permian, the most prolific basin in the United States, is going to be the game-changer for the integrated energy giant. According to the data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, the breakeven price for new wells in the Midland, a sub-basin of the Permian, is $69 per barrel.
